title: ERP Readiness Assessment
intro: This questionnaire helps you assess your organization's readiness before implementing ERP. There are no "right" or "wrong" answers — please select the situation that best describes your current business reality.

questions.text: At which stage is your organization with ERP?

options.text: No ERP yet, considering whether to implement
Decided to implement, looking for solutions/partners
Currently implementing
Live but results below expectations
Live and operating well, want to optimize

questions.text: If you ask 3 employees doing the same critical task — for example, receiving raw materials or approving purchase requests — how would they describe the process?

options.text: Each person does it differently, depending on who's responsible and the situation
Same main steps, but differ significantly on exceptions and approvers
Basically the same; documented process exists but not regularly updated
Same; process is documented, updated, and matches actual practice
I'm not sure

questions.text: If a key person (warehouse manager, accounting chief, production manager, QA lead, etc.) quit suddenly next week, what would happen?

options.text: Some operations halt — the way things work is mostly in their head
Still runs but many errors for months; replacement has to figure it out
Documentation/handover exists; replacement takes weeks to grasp it
Replacement can follow existing procedures, templates, and records with minimal disruption
I'm not sure

questions.text: How are master data — product codes, materials, suppliers, customers — currently managed?

options.text: Each department has its own list; same product called different names by sales, warehouse, finance
One master list but many duplicates, obsolete codes, missing info
Relatively unified, someone owns it, but no clear rules for creating/updating codes
Unified; someone is accountable with clear rules for creating, updating, retiring codes
I'm not sure

questions.text: In management meetings, do inventory, production, and payable figures from different departments align?

options.text: Often misaligned; lots of time debating which number is correct
Usually off; someone manually reconciles before each meeting
Generally aligned; small differences that can be explained
Aligned, single source; inventory is reconciled monthly with physical counts
I'm not sure

questions.text: Where do material specifications (BOM/recipe) and manufacturing sequences currently live?

options.text: Mainly in production manager's or senior worker's head
Documented but doesn't match actual practice, or multiple versions exist
Documented for most products, but updates aren't consistent
Documented for main products, version-controlled, someone is accountable
I'm not sure — doesn't apply (we don't manufacture)

questions.text: Do you know the actual cost and profit margin for each main product line?

options.text: No — only know overall company profit/loss
Have estimates based on experience or old data
Calculate it but compile manually, delayed after close
Yes, using consistent cost allocation, updated monthly
I'm not sure — accounting team handles this

questions.text: For your ERP project (planned or underway), have you defined what "success" means?

options.text: No — vague goals like "better management", "digital transformation"
Yes, but technical: complete modules, go-live on time
Yes, business goals (lower inventory, control costs) but not measurable
Yes, measurable business goals with timeline and owner
I'm not sure

questions.text: How is the initial ERP phase (planned or executed) being approached?

options.text: Big bang all departments at once; software must match our way of working
Multiple modules quickly; customize software where gaps exist
Focus on a few core modules, but unclear who decides on scope changes
Phase 1 is small, documented; ready to adapt to software standards; scope changes go through impact review
I'm not sure

questions.text: What is leadership's role in the ERP project (planned or underway)?

options.text: Hand it to IT or the vendor; leadership approves budget and gets status reports
One leader is responsible but very busy, often absent at critical decisions
Leadership involved in big decisions; department heads lack clear authority and time
Someone with authority dedicates regular time; department heads have clear responsibility and time
I'm not sure

questions.text: Last time your organization changed how it works (new software, new process, new forms), how did the team react?

options.text: Complied briefly then went back to old ways — or no major change recently
Accepted when required, but still use Excel, paper, old ways in parallel
Adapted over time, needed repeated leadership reminders
Adapted well because they understood why, had guidance, and were monitored
I'm not sure

questions.text: For current systems and processes (accounting software, ISO procedures, shared Excel files), who decides on changes and who's accountable?

options.text: Unclear — whoever needs it fixes it, or it waits for leadership
Concentrates on a few (usually IT or finance head), no formal process
Each system has an owner, but changes aren't evaluated for impact or tracked
Clear owner; changes go through propose–evaluate–approve–record
I'm not sure

questions.text: Looking back at your answers: what surprised you most about your organization's actual readiness?

levels.label: Early Stage
levels.description: Your organization lacks the process and data foundation to make ERP valuable immediately. Next logical step: standardize processes before evaluating software.

levels.label: Developing
levels.description: Some foundation exists but consistency is lacking. Biggest risk if you implement ERP now: scope creep and messy data.

levels.label: Fairly Ready
levels.description: Most conditions are met. Before finalizing scope, carefully address remaining gaps.

levels.label: Ready
levels.description: Your organization has a solid foundation for successful ERP implementation. Now focus on right scope and timeline.
